law_scope.statutory_version: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 as applied to the 1967 eviction petition described in the supplied judgment

cases.target_stage: Supreme Court civil appeal by certificate under Article 133 (Civil Appeal No. 1297 of 1975)
cases.substantive_issue: Whether unauthorized sub-letting without the landlord's consent under Section 14(1)(b) had been established; the Supreme Court expressly treated sub-letting as substantiated but did not reproduce the underlying evidentiary analysis.

issue_refs.quote: The eviction petition set out two grounds out of the many specified in cite21†s. 14 of the Rent Act, viz.,unauthorized sub-letting of a portion of the premises and possession, by the tenant, of alternative accommodation.

The Rent Controller, at the floor level, ordered eviction and the Appellate Tribunal affirmed it, upholding the vice of sub-letting without consent of the landlord in the manner specified in cite23†s. 14(1)(b)

allowed_spans.quote: The appellant is the tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent- landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954
allowed_spans.reason: Neutral tenancy background preceding the target-court application.

allowed_spans.quote: The landlord had been receiving rent from the tenant until the time he filed a petition for eviction (1967)
allowed_spans.reason: Neutral chronology fixing the eviction-petition context.

allowed_spans.quote: The eviction petition set out two grounds out of the many specified in cite21†s. 14 of the Rent Act, viz.,unauthorized sub-letting of a portion of the premises and possession, by the tenant, of alternative accommodation.
allowed_spans.reason: Exact statement of the landlord's pleaded sub-letting ground without converting the target court's endorsement into a factual span.

excluded_stage_notes: The Supreme Court's detailed merits reasoning principally concerns determination/forfeiture of the lease under the Transfer of Property Act and justice, equity and good conscience; those target-stage passages are not converted into allowed factual spans.

law_scope.provision: Section 2(1) tenant definition / heritability of commercial statutory tenancy
law_scope.statutory_version: Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 including the retrospective amendment by Act 18 of 1976 discussed in the supplied judgment

cases.target_stage: Supreme Court appeal by special leave
cases.substantive_issue: Whether a statutory tenancy in commercial premises is heritable and whether the heirs of a deceased tenant remain protected by the Delhi Rent Control Act.

issue_refs.quote: The question for consideration in this appeal by special leave is whether under the cite14†Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 (for the sake of brevity hereinafter referred to as the Act), the statutory tenancy to use the popular phraseology, in respect of commercial premises is heritable or not.

To state is more precisely, the question is whether the heirs of a deceased tenant whose contractual tenancy in respect of commercial premises has been determined, are entitled to the same protection against eviction afforded by the Act to the tenant.

application_refs.quote: The tenancy right of Wasti Ram, therefore, devolves on all the heirs of Wasti Ram on his death.
The heirs and legal representatives of Wasti Ram step into his position and they are entitled to the benefit and protection of the Act.

excluded_stage_notes.note: The Rent Controller's statement that sub-letting had been established is a lower-court outcome only; detailed reasoning is not quoted.
The Rent Control Tribunal remanded the sub-letting question for fresh decision after evidence; it did not supply a final detailed application finding usable as a target issue here.
The Supreme Court remanded the appeal and cross-objection on merits after deciding heritability; it did not adjudicate the sub-letting merits.

coverage_gaps: The only merits issue actually decided by the target court is heritability/protection of commercial statutory tenancy, which is outside the allowed families.
The allowed-family sub-letting question remained for merits determination after remand and lacks detailed quoted lower-court reasoning.

law_scope.statute: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952
law_scope.statutory_version: Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952 as applied to the post-commencement 1954 sub-tenancy described in the supplied judgment

cases.target_stage: Supreme Court civil appeal by special leave (relevant discussion in Civil Appeal No. 464 of 1971)
cases.substantive_issue: As an intermediate statutory application in the standard-rent limitation dispute, whether the appellant's post-Act induction as a sub-tenant lacked the landlord's written consent contemplated by Section 13(1)(b) before the landlord later accepted him as a direct tenant.

issue_refs.quote: where the sub-tenant has been inducted after the commencement of the Act which is the situation in the present case, the tenant does not include a sub-tenant because cite18†Section 13(1)(b) removes the protection of a tenant against eviction if after the commencement of the Act he has sub-let or assigned or otherwise parted with possession without obtaining the consent of the landlord in writing.

application_refs.quote: Appellant was inducted as a sub-tenant after the commencement of the Act and there is no evidence to show that he was so inducted with the written consent of the landlord.
Admitedly, the appellant was inducted as sub-tenant by the head-tenant Mr. Brook.
Brook surrendered his tenancy the sub-tenant was accepted as tenant of the premises by the landlord with effect from May 1, 1955 with some increase in the monthly rent.

allowed_spans.quote: A bungalow with an attached cottage situated at No. 1, Hailey Road, New Delhi was taken on lease by one E. B. Brook and he inducted the appellant as a sub-tenant in the cottage portion
allowed_spans.reason: Neutral record of the head-tenant/sub-tenant relationship before the target-court analysis.

allowed_spans.quote: Appellant did not vacate the premises in his possession but reached an agreement with Lakhmir Singh, the then landlord on June 20/22, 1955 to become the direct tenant of the then landlord of the premises in his possession
allowed_spans.reason: Documents the later direct-tenancy arrangement, preserving the temporal boundary after the earlier sub-tenancy.

allowed_spans.quote: Appellant was inducted as a sub-tenant on September 1, 1954 1 by the head-tenant.
allowed_spans.reason: Exact pre-target chronology of the sub-tenancy.

allowed_spans.quote: The head-tenant surrendered his tenancy and vacated and handed over possession of the portion of premises in his possession on April 1, 1955.
allowed_spans.reason: Neutral event marking the end of the head tenancy.

allowed_spans.quote: In June 1955 appellant and the landlord arrived at an agreement Ex. P-2 by which appellant was accepted a direct tenant of the premises in his possession from May 1, 1955 on a monthly rent of Rs. 269. 50 p.
allowed_spans.reason: Documented subsequent direct tenancy relevant to distinguishing the earlier sub-tenancy period.

excluded_stage_notes: The principal appeal issue is limitation for a standard-rent application under Sections 8 and 11(b); the Section 13(1)(b) discussion is only an intermediate application bearing on when the appellant became a protected tenant.
The target court's no-written-consent and admitted-sub-tenancy statements are application_refs and are excluded from allowed_spans.
No eviction claim under Section 13(1)(b) is finally adjudicated in this appeal.
coverage_gaps: The supplied judgment does not reproduce any underlying consent document or testimony; it only states that there was no evidence of written consent.
Because Section 13(1)(b) is used within a limitation analysis rather than to dispose of a sub-letting eviction ground, the example is suitable only for locally supervised condition annotation.

law_scope.statutory_version: NDMC Act, 1994 as applied to the NDMC (Determination of Annual Rent) Bye-laws, 2009

cases.target_stage: Supreme Court civil appeals arising out of special leave petitions
cases.substantive_issue: Whether the 2009 NDMC Unit Area Method bye-laws were ultra vires Section 63 of the NDMC Act because they determined rateable value by property value rather than the statutorily required annual letting rent.

issue_refs.quote: In the first place, we take up the fundamental issue, namely, whether the impugned Bye-laws are ultra vires Section 63 of the NDMC Act?

application_refs.quote: After going through the Bye-laws and the manner in which the rateable value is fixed, we are constrained to observe that it is not in sink with the scheme of Section 63(1) of the NDMC Act.
Such Bye-laws are, thus, ultra vires the provisions of NDMC Act. They are in excess of the scope and ambit of powers vested in the NDMC Act under Section 388(1)(A)(9) of the NDMC Act.

excluded_stage_notes: References to the Delhi Rent Control Act concern the standard-rent ceiling used in municipal property-tax valuation, not an adjudicated DRC sub-letting or bona fide requirement issue.
Mentions of letting and sub-letting in Sections 66-67 of the NDMC Act concern incidence/apportionment of property tax, not landlord-tenant eviction conditions.
The target court expressly declined to decide the other challenges to the bye-laws after resolving the ultra vires issue.
coverage_gaps: No allowed-family substantive issue is adjudicated by the target court.
The case is a municipal property-tax / delegated-legislation dispute, outside DRC_SUBLETTING, DRC_BONA_FIDE, and LEASE_LICENCE.
